description: A 15-minute impromptu-speaking section of every club meeting: the Hot Questions Master poses unexpected questions and members deliver 1-2 minute spontaneous answers on the spot, with no preparation. The Agora equivalent of Toastmasters' Table Topics; canonical impromptu/quick-wit drill of the format.
The first basic-path project: deliver a very short introductory speech to the club to take your first step into public speaking. Equivalent to an Ice Breaker; goal is to simply stand up and speak.
Basic-path project where the speaker delivers a short speech about a topic of personal interest, to build comfort speaking from genuine enthusiasm and personal material.
Basic-path self-introduction project where the speaker tells the club who they are, building self-disclosure and personal storytelling skills.

Basic-path project teaching how to structure a speech (opening, body, close). Most basic-path projects have two parts done in separate meetings: a speech-analysis part (dissect an accomplished speaker's structure) and a delivery part (deliver a speech applying the technique).
Basic-path project focused on crafting and delivering a speech with a single clear central message/takeaway.
Basic-path project where the speaker delivers a speech deliberately varying pitch, pace, volume, and pauses to keep the audience engaged through vocal dynamics.

Basic-path project where the speaker delivers a speech consciously using gestures, posture, movement, and facial expression to reinforce the message. A Body Language Evaluator gives targeted feedback.
Basic-path project where the speaker researches an unfamiliar subject and delivers an informed speech on it, building credibility through evidence.
Basic-path project on developing/expanding ideas within a speech so each point is fully fleshed out rather than merely stated.
Basic-path project where the speaker tailors a speech to a specific audience, practising audience analysis and adapting content/tone accordingly.
Basic-path project where the speaker delivers a speech supported by slides/visual aids, practising integrating presentation software without being dominated by it.
Basic-path project in the 'Speaking Techniques' group requiring the speaker to deliver a speech under added constraints/handling difficult content, building adaptability.
Basic-path 'Speaking Techniques' project where the speaker deliberately incorporates humour into a speech to entertain and connect with the audience.
Basic-path 'Speaking Techniques' project where the speaker weaves anecdotes/short stories into a speech to illustrate points and build rapport.
Basic-path 'Speaking Techniques' project where the speaker delivers a speech crafted to evoke emotion in the audience, practising emotional resonance and pathos.
Final basic-path project where the speaker brings together all techniques into a polished delivery with command of the stage; capstone of the basic path.

A recurring meeting activity and the first half of most basic-path projects: the member studies/dissects an accomplished speaker's speech (structure, message, technique) and reports what made it work, before later delivering their own speech applying that technique.

After each prepared speech, a designated Speech Evaluator explains the project's objectives beforehand and delivers a 3-5 minute spoken evaluation afterward, giving the speaker structured strengths/improvements feedback. Evaluating is itself a trained speaking skill.
A meeting activity in which a designated speaker presents a short talk transporting the audience to a place/culture/destination, practising vivid descriptive and informative speaking.

A meeting activity where a Crossfire Presenter takes a position and is rapidly questioned/challenged by the audience, training the speaker to think and respond under pressure and defend a viewpoint live.
A structured in-meeting debate (Debate Moderator, Debate Participants, Debate Judge) where members argue opposing sides of a motion, training persuasive and impromptu argumentation.

A moderated panel/discussion meeting activity (Colloquium Moderator, Participants, Evaluator) where members discuss a topic conversationally in front of the club, training discussion and conversational speaking.
A meeting activity in which members act out an assigned scenario/role in front of the club, practising spontaneous character and situational speaking.
A short meeting activity designed to spark creativity/spontaneity in members through a playful prompt or game before/between speeches.
In-meeting word/language games run by a Language Improvement Leader (alongside the Grammarian and Filler Word Counter roles) to sharpen vocabulary, grammar, and elimination of filler words.
A meeting activity where a member opens with a brief reflective thought/quote and a short comment on it, practising concise prepared micro-speaking.
A 21-project (incl. capstone) advanced path unlocked after the basic path, dedicated to developing the speaker into a storyteller. Real-world application required (performing outside the home club).
An advanced path of projects developing the speaker as a comedian/entertainer through humorous-speech assignments.
An advanced path of projects training the speaker to deliver persuasive/argumentative speeches that move an audience to a position or action.
An advanced path of projects for occasion speaking (toasts, eulogies, introductions, acceptance speeches, etc.).
An advanced path training theatrical/dramatic performance and character work in speeches.

A 10-project advanced path of speaking challenges with playful constraints (named projects: Failure, Hecklers, Twisted Geometry, Time Warp, Duplicates, The Silent Towns, Emptiness, Who Stole My Cheese, Late to the Party, plus a Capstone) that force the speaker to adapt to adverse/unexpected conditions.
An official Agora contest in which members compete by delivering a story; culminates in a world final. A performance-as-practice format for storytelling.

An official Agora contest where members deliver a humorous speech (max 7 minutes, props optional). At country level and above, judges are non-Agora media professionals, comedians, and pro speakers. Goal: find excellent comedians/entertainers.

Solo practice mode where the user improvises a scene against an AI partner that responds to the user's choices and adjusts to their style and skill level; the user can explore characters and build scenes anytime without a human partner. The app's flagship AI feature.
Solo practice mode giving the user game-specific prompts and timed activities to develop monologues, characters, and storytelling skills independently.
Two-player practice mode that walks a pair through structured improv games targeting specific skills, with clear turn-based instructions to guide the session.
Two-player scene-building mode using relationship prompts so a pair can create scenes, develop characters, and strengthen active-listening skills.
Any-size tool that quickly generates random audience suggestions (locations, relationships, scenarios) to kick-start an improv scene.
Any-size tool that generates random words to spark creativity and build quick-thinking/association skills.
Core pair exercise (Beginner): two players build a scene by each accepting the prior offer and adding new information with 'Yes, and...', the foundational improv drill.
Core solo exercise (Beginner): the user practises a tight three-line exchange that establishes a relationship/scene economically.
Core solo exercise (Beginner-Intermediate): the user mimes handling invisible objects to build space-work and physical-detail skills.
Core pair exercise (Beginner) drilling enthusiastic acceptance/agreement between partners.
Core pair exercise (Beginner) that pushes players to keep adding detail and offers to a scene rather than ending early.
Core pair exercise (Intermediate) training players to find and sustain an emotional/thematic underscore beneath a scene.
Core solo exercise (Intermediate): the user tells/performs a story to an empty chair, practising solo narrative and presence.
Core pair exercise (Intermediate) drilling shifts between distinct emotional states mapped to positions/squares.
Core group exercise (Beginner) where players create characters by leading their movement with a specific body part, building physical character work.
Core pair exercise (Intermediate-Advanced) where players perform a scene that switches genres on cue, training tonal flexibility.
Core pair exercise (Beginner): an associative listing/building game packing a picnic basket, drilling agreement and memory.
Core group exercise (Intermediate): players collaboratively pitch/sell an absurd product, building heightening and group agreement.
Fun-and-games pair exercise (Intermediate): on the call 'new choice' the player must instantly replace their last line/action with a different one, drilling spontaneity and letting go.
Fun-and-games group exercise (Intermediate-Advanced) where a 'director' restarts/redirects a scene, training adaptability to direction.
Fun-and-games group exercise (Beginner-Intermediate): players cycle through scenes on a park bench, each entering with a strong character, drilling character initiation.
Fun-and-games group exercise (Intermediate): a player is interviewed as a fabricated 'expert' and must answer questions confidently and spontaneously.
Fun-and-games pair exercise (Beginner-Intermediate) drilling supportive agreement / building on a partner's contributions.
Fun-and-games pair exercise (Intermediate-Advanced): players must incorporate pre-written/random lines into a scene, drilling justification and quick integration.
Solo warm-up (Beginner): rapid free-association from word to word to loosen up and build quick thinking.
Solo warm-up (Beginner): articulation/diction warm-up using tongue twisters before practice.
Pair warm-up (Beginner): partners count 1-2-3 alternately then progressively replace numbers with gestures/sounds, a classic focus-and-coordination warm-up.
Pair warm-up (Beginner): players pull endless imaginary objects from a box and justify them, drilling spontaneity and object work.
Group warm-up (Intermediate): a fast spoken articulation/passing game, energising the group and sharpening verbal agility.
Group warm-up (Beginner): a fast pointing/naming reaction game in a circle, building focus and quick response under pressure.
Group warm-up (Beginner): players mirror each other's character/movement in a circle, building physical attunement and ensemble.

exercise_name: Pointing To Things in the Room
description: Group warm-up (Beginner-Intermediate): players point at objects and call them by wrong names, drilling letting-go and breaking habitual associations.
Group warm-up (Beginner): a high-energy circle elimination/reaction game in a Wild West theme, building focus and play.
Group warm-up (Beginner): players rapidly list eight things about a prompt while the group counts, drilling commitment and not over-thinking.
Group warm-up (Beginner-Intermediate): a player in the centre is tagged in/out and must immediately start a song/association, drilling spontaneity under spotlight.
Group warm-up (Beginner): an escalating-energy circle game building group focus and shared rhythm.
